newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: No U.S. stock market crash in sight, UBS says.
newsitem.headline: No U.S. stock market crash in sight, UBS says.

text.p: Contrary to popular belief, the U.S. stock market is not on the verge of a crash or even major correction, Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) said on Tuesday.
Based on price earnings (PE) ratios, the U.S. equity markets were only slightly overvalued at the moment, a group of UBS economists told a briefing in Singapore.

Several economists have said this year the New York stock market was heading for a fall in a correction to an almost uninterrupted bull-run which has taken the Dow Jones Industrial Average to around 6,000 points from 3,600 at the end of 1994.

UBS chief international economist George Magnus said the firm thought the United States economy would show slower growth in 1997 than in 1996 and this would put pressure on corporate earnings and encourage some extra weighting in bond markets.
This meant the Dow would flatten out and may not see much growth over in 1997. But it did not mean a crash was coming.
"Our view is that we are on the cusp of a protracted period of below trend growth in the United States," Magnus said.
"We will see a slowdown in 1997 to around 1.8 percent (real) growth (in gross domestic product) from 2.3 percent in 1996."
"But we are not looking for a (19)87 style crash," said Chris Carter, the head of global equities strategy at UBS.

"On a PE basis, the (U.S.) market is a little high, that's why (the Dow) is having problems getting through 6,000 points," he said. However, the likely implication of this was that the New York market would merely stall.
"The U.S. market is probably going nowhere," he said.
Carter said UBS expected the Dow to stay close to its current level of about 6,000 points until early 1997 and said it may remain at that level for the rest of the following year.
He said the Japanese market was also unlikely to make any spectacular gains but would probably rise towards around 22,000 points on the Nikkei average from its current level of about 21,000 points.
"Think about cutting back at 22,000 and certainly underweighting if it gets to 23,000," he said.
Larry Hatheway, UBS's chief East Asia economist, said he was a long-term bull on Asia outside Japan and particularly for economies such as Hong Kong and Singapore.
But he said the current cyclical downturn across Asia, which has recently afflicted many Southeast Asian economies, was set to continue until at least the middle of 1997.

"The recovery is going to depend critically on a recovery in export markets...in the U.S. and, the other major G7 economies and in Japan," he said, warning, "If growth falters in Japan, the recovery in (Southeast) Asia will be delayed."
"The risk is on the downside, ie it may come later rather than sooner," he said.
G7 groups Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
Carter said UBS recommended investors move to a neutral position on Asia outside Japan.
The only area UBS was very positive on was Europe. It recommended investors to stay overweight in British equities and also to consider looking at other European bourses such as Germany.
